question: Using (i) the consolidated statements of income and (ii) the interest income/expense table, quantify how much of the 2022→2023 increase in total net revenue was explained by the increase in net interest income. Then compute net interest income as a percentage of total net revenue for 2021, 2022, and 2023, and state whether the revenue mix shifted meaningfully toward net interest income over the three-year period.
answer: Net interest income rose from $66,710MM (2022) to $89,267MM (2023), an increase of $22,557MM. Total net revenue rose from $128,695MM to $158,104MM, an increase of $29,409MM. So about $22,557MM / $29,409MM ≈ 76.7% of the revenue increase was explained by higher net interest income. Net interest income as a share of total net revenue was ~56.8% in 2021 (52,311 / 121,649), ~51.8% in 2022 (66,710 / 128,695), and ~56.5% in 2023 (89,267 / 158,104). The mix shifted down in 2022 but shifted back up in 2023; across 2021→2023 it ended roughly where it started (mid-56%), so the three-year shift is not monotonic but 2023 marks a meaningful re-tilt toward net interest income versus 2022.
justification: The interest income/expense table reports net interest income for 2021–2023, while the income statement/segment totals provide total net revenue for the same years. Comparing the changes from 2022 to 2023 isolates the portion of revenue growth attributable to net interest income. Computing NII divided by total net revenue for each year evaluates mix shift over time.

question: NVIDIA discloses inventory reserve expense amounts in cost of revenue for fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2023. Compute inventory reserve expense as a percentage of cost of revenue for each of those two years, and quantify the year-over-year increase in both dollars and percentage points.
answer: Inventory reserve expense was approximately $1.04 billion in FY2023 and $173 million in FY2022. As a percentage of cost of revenue, this is ~9.0% in FY2023 ($1,040 / $11,618) versus ~1.8% in FY2022 ($173 / $9,439). The reserve expense increased by about $867 million year-over-year and rose by roughly 7.1 percentage points (about 9.0% − 1.8%).
justification: The notes disclose inventory reserve expense recorded in cost of revenue for FY2023 and FY2022. Cost of revenue amounts are disclosed in the consolidated statements of income. Dividing reserve expense by cost of revenue yields the implied reserve burden on gross margin for each year and allows a clean year-over-year comparison.

question: Using NVIDIA’s revenue by geographic invoicing address for fiscal 2021–2023, reconcile the near-flat total revenue from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2023 by attributing the $60 million net change to each geography. Then determine (a) which geography contributed the most to revenue growth, (b) which two geographies together contributed the largest offsetting decline, and (c) whether the U.S. became a majority or minority of revenue in fiscal 2023.
answer: FY2022→FY2023 changes (in millions): United States +$3,943 (8,292 − 4,349); Taiwan −$1,558 (6,986 − 8,544); China −$1,326 (5,785 − 7,111); Other countries −$999 (5,911 − 6,910). These sum to +$60, matching total revenue’s net change. (a) The United States contributed the most to growth (+$3,943). (b) Taiwan + China together contributed the largest offsetting decline (−$2,884). (c) The U.S. remained a minority of revenue in FY2023: $8,292 out of $26,974 is ~30.7%, so revenue outside the U.S. (~69.3%) was still the majority.
justification: The geographic revenue table provides revenues for the United States, Taiwan, China (including Hong Kong), and other countries for FY2023/FY2022/FY2021 along with the total. Subtracting FY2022 from FY2023 for each line item reconciles the net total change and reveals which geographies drove growth versus decline. The U.S. share is computed by dividing U.S. revenue by total revenue for FY2023.

question: Using Exxon Mobil’s consolidated statement of income for 2021–2023, compute the effective income tax rate for each year (income tax expense divided by income before income taxes). Then determine (a) which year had the highest effective tax rate and (b) by how many percentage points the effective tax rate changed from 2021 to 2023.
answer: Effective tax rates were approximately 29.2% (2023), 25.9% (2022), and 24.4% (2021). (a) 2023 had the highest effective tax rate. (b) The effective tax rate increased by about 4.8 percentage points from 2021 (~24.4%) to 2023 (~29.2%).
justification: From the consolidated statement of income: 2023 income before income taxes was $52,783 million and income tax expense was $15,429 million, giving ~15,429/52,783 = 29.2%. For 2022, $20,176 million tax on $77,753 million pretax income gives ~25.9%. For 2021, $7,636 million tax on $31,234 million pretax income gives ~24.4%. Comparing years shows the effective rate peaks in 2023 and rises by ~29.2% − 24.4% ≈ 4.8 percentage points from 2021 to 2023.

question: Using the consolidated statement of cash flows and consolidated statement of income for 2021–2023, compute ExxonMobil’s operating cash-flow conversion ratio for each year, defined as net cash provided by operating activities divided by net income attributable to ExxonMobil. Then explain which year shows the strongest conversion and why that matters for interpreting earnings quality over the period.
answer: Operating cash-flow conversion ratios were approximately 1.54x (2023), 1.38x (2022), and 2.09x (2021). The strongest conversion was in 2021 (~2.09x), indicating operating cash generation exceeded accounting earnings by the widest margin that year, which can signal stronger non-cash addbacks and/or more favorable working-capital movements relative to reported earnings.
justification: Net cash provided by operating activities was $55,369 million (2023), $76,797 million (2022), and $48,129 million (2021). Net income attributable to ExxonMobil was $36,010 million (2023), $55,740 million (2022), and $23,040 million (2021). Dividing yields ~1.54x, ~1.38x, and ~2.09x respectively. The interpretation matters because higher conversion indicates more cash backing each dollar of earnings; over multi-year comparisons, it helps distinguish margin-driven earnings from cash-backed performance.

question: ExxonMobil presents a non-GAAP metric, "cash flow from operations and asset sales," and separately reports shareholder distributions through cash dividends to ExxonMobil shareholders and common stock acquired. For each of 2021–2023, compute shareholder distributions as a percentage of cash flow from operations and asset sales. Then identify the year with the highest payout intensity and quantify how much higher it was than the lowest year (in percentage points).
answer: Shareholder distributions as a percentage of cash flow from operations and asset sales were approximately 55.0% (2023), 36.7% (2022), and 29.4% (2021). The highest payout intensity was 2023 (~55.0%), which was about 25.6 percentage points higher than the lowest year, 2021 (~29.4%).
justification: Cash flow from operations and asset sales was $59,447 million (2023), $82,044 million (2022), and $51,305 million (2021). Shareholder distributions are cash dividends to ExxonMobil shareholders plus common stock acquired: 2023 $14,941 + $17,748 = $32,689 million; 2022 $14,939 + $15,155 = $30,094 million; 2021 $14,924 + $155 = $15,079 million. Ratios are ~32,689/59,447 = 55.0%, ~30,094/82,044 = 36.7%, and ~15,079/51,305 = 29.4%. The spread between the highest (2023) and lowest (2021) is ~55.0% − 29.4% ≈ 25.6 percentage points.

question: Using ExxonMobil’s consolidated balance sheet, compute net debt at December 31, 2023 and December 31, 2022, defined as (notes and loans payable + long-term debt) minus (cash and cash equivalents + restricted cash and cash equivalents). Then quantify the year-over-year change in net debt and state whether ExxonMobil delevered or relevered in 2023.
answer: Net debt was approximately $10.0B at December 31, 2023 and $11.5B at December 31, 2022, a decrease of about $1.5B year-over-year. ExxonMobil therefore delevered in 2023 on this net-debt definition.
justification: Balance sheet amounts (in $ millions): 2023 notes and loans payable $4,090 and long-term debt $37,483 (total debt $41,573); cash and cash equivalents $31,539 and restricted cash $29 (total cash $31,568). Net debt 2023 = 41,573 − 31,568 = 10,005 (~$10.0B). For 2022, notes and loans payable $634 plus long-term debt $40,559 (total debt $41,193); cash $29,640 plus restricted cash $25 (total cash $29,665). Net debt 2022 = 41,193 − 29,665 = 11,528 (~$11.5B). Net debt fell by 11,528 − 10,005 = 1,523 (~$1.5B), indicating deleveraging.

question: ExxonMobil reports ROCE (non-GAAP) as earnings excluding financing costs divided by average capital employed. Using the ROCE table for 2021–2023, (a) compute ROCE for each year using the reported earnings excluding financing costs and average capital employed, and (b) determine how much of the ROCE decline from 2022 to 2023 is explained by the change in the numerator (earnings excluding financing costs) versus the change in the denominator (average capital employed), holding the other variable constant (use a simple bridge: first change numerator at 2022 denominator, then change denominator).
answer: (a) ROCE is approximately 15.0% (2023), 24.9% (2022), and 10.9% (2021). (b) From 2022 to 2023, ROCE fell ~9.9 percentage points (24.9% to 15.0%). Holding the 2022 denominator constant, the numerator drop alone would reduce ROCE from ~24.9% to ~16.0% (about −8.9 pp). The denominator increase then reduces it further from ~16.0% to ~15.0% (about −1.0 pp). So most of the decline is driven by lower earnings excluding financing costs, with a smaller contribution from higher average capital employed.
justification: The ROCE table provides earnings excluding financing costs of $56,875 million (2022) and $36,561 million (2023) and average capital employed of $228,404 million (2022) and $243,440 million (2023). ROCE computed: 2022 = 56,875/228,404 ≈ 24.9%; 2023 = 36,561/243,440 ≈ 15.0%; 2021 = 24,395/222,890 ≈ 10.9%. Bridge: Replace numerator first: 36,561/228,404 ≈ 16.0% (a drop of ~8.9 pp vs 24.9%). Then replace denominator: 36,561/243,440 ≈ 15.0% (a further ~1.0 pp drop).

question: ExxonMobil provides "earnings (loss) excluding identified items" (non-GAAP) alongside GAAP net income attributable to ExxonMobil. Using the corporate total reconciliation for 2021–2023, compute the identified-items impact in each year as (non-GAAP earnings excluding identified items minus GAAP net income). Then determine which year had the largest negative identified-items impact and by how much it differed from 2023 (in $ billions).
answer: Identified-items impacts were approximately +$2.6B (2023), +$3.4B (2022), and about −$0.0B (2021; roughly +$0.0B given a small net +$0.03B identified-items total). The largest negative identified-items total (i.e., largest drag embedded in GAAP vs non-GAAP) occurred in 2022 at about $3.4B, which was about $0.8B larger than 2023’s ~$2.6B impact.
justification: Corporate total GAAP net income attributable to ExxonMobil is $36,010 million (2023), $55,740 million (2022), and $23,040 million (2021). Earnings excluding identified items are $38,572 million (2023), $59,101 million (2022), and $23,013 million (2021). Differences are 38,572 − 36,010 = 2,562 million (~$2.6B) in 2023; 59,101 − 55,740 = 3,361 million (~$3.4B) in 2022; and 23,013 − 23,040 = −27 million (~−$0.0B) in 2021. Thus 2022 shows the largest gap between GAAP and the underlying earnings measure, exceeding 2023 by about 3.361 − 2.562 = 0.799 billion dollars (~$0.8B).

question: Using the segment earnings table (GAAP) and the corporate total GAAP net income attributable to ExxonMobil for 2021–2023, compute (a) Upstream’s share of corporate net income and (b) Energy Products’ share of corporate net income for each year. Then explain, based on those computed shares, how the earnings mix shifted from 2021 to 2023.
answer: Upstream’s share of corporate net income was ~68.5% (2021), ~65.4% (2022), and ~59.2% (2023). Energy Products’ share was about −1.5% (2021), ~26.8% (2022), and ~33.7% (2023). The mix shifted toward Energy Products and away from Upstream between 2021 and 2023, with Energy Products moving from a loss in 2021 to a large positive contributor by 2022–2023 while Upstream’s dominance moderated by 2023.
justification: Segment earnings (GAAP) are: Upstream 15,775 (2021), 36,479 (2022), 21,308 (2023); Energy Products (347) (2021), 14,966 (2022), 12,142 (2023). Corporate GAAP net income attributable to ExxonMobil is 23,040 (2021), 55,740 (2022), 36,010 (2023). Dividing gives Upstream shares: 15,775/23,040 ≈ 68.5%; 36,479/55,740 ≈ 65.4%; 21,308/36,010 ≈ 59.2%. Energy Products shares: −347/23,040 ≈ −1.5%; 14,966/55,740 ≈ 26.8%; 12,142/36,010 ≈ 33.7%. This indicates a clear shift toward downstream Energy Products earnings contribution post-2021, while Upstream contribution declines in relative terms by 2023.

question: Using the "Production Prices and Production Costs" table for 2021–2023, estimate a simplified upstream unit margin proxy each year as (total average crude oil price per barrel minus total average production costs per oil-equivalent barrel). Then compare the change in this proxy from 2022 to 2023 with the change in Upstream GAAP earnings over the same period and explain what the comparison suggests about the role of commodity pricing versus other drivers.
answer: Simplified unit-margin proxies are approximately $56.0 (2021), $84.5 (2022), and $67.3 (2023) per unit (price minus cost). From 2022 to 2023, the proxy fell by about $17.2 (from ~$84.5 to ~$67.3), while Upstream GAAP earnings fell by $15.2B (from $36.479B to $21.308B). The broad alignment suggests commodity price/cost dynamics were a major headwind in 2023 versus 2022, though the magnitude difference indicates other factors (e.g., volumes, mix, non-price effects, or identified items within Upstream) also influenced earnings.
justification: Total average crude oil prices were $66.96 (2021), $95.88 (2022), and $77.92 (2023) per barrel. Total average production costs were $10.92 (2021), $11.43 (2022), and $10.63 (2023) per oil-equivalent barrel. Subtracting yields proxies: 2021 ~66.96 − 10.92 = 56.04; 2022 ~95.88 − 11.43 = 84.45; 2023 ~77.92 − 10.63 = 67.29. The 2022→2023 decline is ~17.16. Upstream GAAP earnings declined from $36,479 million (2022) to $21,308 million (2023), a drop of $15,171 million. This supports the interpretation that pricing normalization from 2022’s elevated levels drove much of the earnings decline, with additional operational/portfolio factors contributing.

question: Using (i) ExxonMobil’s total oil-equivalent proved reserves and (ii) oil-equivalent production, estimate a proved reserve life index (RLI) for 2023 and 2021, defined as total proved reserves (million boe) divided by annual oil-equivalent production (million boe, computed from thousands of boe per day × 365). Then compute how many years the RLI changed from 2021 to 2023 and interpret what that implies about reserve replacement relative to production over the period.
answer: Estimated proved RLI was about 12.4 years in 2023 and about 13.7 years in 2021, a decline of roughly 1.3 years. This implies that, over 2021–2023, proved reserves fell relative to production pace, indicating reserve replacement (net of revisions, acquisitions/dispositions, and extensions) did not fully keep up with produced volumes on this simplified metric.
justification: Total proved reserves (oil-equivalent, all products) were 16,928 million boe at December 31, 2023 and 18,536 million boe at December 31, 2021. Oil-equivalent production was 3,738 thousand boe/day in 2023 and 3,712 thousand boe/day in 2021. Annual production is ~3,738×365/1,000 = 1,364 million boe (2023) and ~3,712×365/1,000 = 1,355 million boe (2021). RLI is ~16,928/1,364 = 12.4 years (2023) and ~18,536/1,355 = 13.7 years (2021). The change is ~12.4 − 13.7 = −1.3 years.
